reference_patient.definition: the typical patient: the median training patient for every number and the most common training category for every category (not a real patient)

confidence_rules.clearly: a meaningful change in predicted risk for a typical patient (at least 5% points), the test split agrees (same sign, and its bootstrap interval over test patients excludes no benefit), and every group has at least 20 training patients
confidence_rules.consistently across patients: the claim holds for at least 90% of training patients (range across patients); this is not a significance statement
confidence_rules.on the training data only: the test split disagrees (opposite sign, or no benefit on test patients) or is unclear (its interval includes no benefit), or no test check is available
confidence_rules.slightly: the change in predicted risk for a typical patient is below 5% points
confidence_rules.the model has little data on this: a compared group has fewer than 20 training patients

settings.effect_scale: log-odds (output pre-activation) for verification; predicted risk for the typical patient for wording

summary.text: The model treats a higher capital gains as clearly lowering the predicted chance of an income of $50,000 or less slowly at first, then faster for most people, but for people whose marital status is never married it moves in stages: for a typical person, it goes from about 53% at 0 US dollars to about 6% at 6849 US dollars, flattening out near the bottom because the predicted risk cannot go much lower.

For a typical person, the model gives a higher predicted chance of an income of $50,000 or less if the country of birth is Guatemala (about 99%) than if country of birth is something other than Cambodia, Guatemala, Haiti, Honduras, India, Canada, Ireland, Italy, Jamaica, Japan, Nicaragua, Peru, China, the Philippines, Scotland, 'South' (as recorded), England (about 53%) (on the training data only).

For a typical person, the model gives a higher predicted chance of an income of $50,000 or less if the country of birth is Nicaragua (about 96%) than if country of birth is something other than Cambodia, Guatemala, Haiti, Honduras, India, Canada, Ireland, Italy, Jamaica, Japan, Nicaragua, Peru, China, the Philippines, Scotland, 'South' (as recorded), England (about 53%) (on the training data only).

A higher age clearly lowers the predicted chance of an income of $50,000 or less, and even more so if occupation is something other than other service (steadily up to about 37 years, then no further for people with occupation other than other service): for a typical person, age going from 22 years to 58 years moves the predicted chance of an income of $50,000 or less from about 87% to about 51% if occupation is something other than other service, and from about 85% to about 84% if the occupation is other service.

For a typical person, going from country of birth other than Guatemala to Guatemala moves the predicted chance of an income of $50,000 or less from about 66% to above 99% if the work class is self-employed, not incorporated, and from about 53% to about 99% if work class is something other than self-employed, not incorporated.
The model ignores census sampling weight.
